days.title: Long Division and Place Value
days.target: I can divide multi-digit whole numbers and check the quotient.
days.lecture: Estimate the quotient first. Divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down one digit at a time. Keep each quotient digit in its place; write zero when needed. Check dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder.

examples.q: Use long division: 138 ÷ 6. Show the algorithm and check.
examples.steps: 13 ÷ 6: write 2, subtract 12, remainder 1; bring down the next digit: 18 ÷ 6: write 3, subtract 18, remainder 0. Check: 6 × 23 = 138.

examples.q: Use long division: 12,183 ÷ 34. Show the algorithm and check.

days.title: Greatest Common Factors
days.target: I can find the greatest common factor and interpret equal groups.
days.lecture: List factor pairs or use prime factorizations. The greatest factor shared by both numbers is the GCF. For identical kits with no leftovers, the GCF gives the greatest number of kits.

examples.q: Find the GCF of 12 and 16. Show factor pairs or prime factors.
examples.steps: Common factors: 1, 2, 4; greatest is 4.

examples.q: Make the greatest possible number of identical kits from 18 pencils and 30 erasers with no leftovers. Find the number of kits and each kit’s contents.
examples.steps: GCF(18, 30) = 6; divide both counts by 6.

days.title: Questions That Anticipate Variability
days.target: I can recognize a statistical question and the expected variability.
days.lecture: A statistical question anticipates different answers in a collection of data. Name the group, the measured attribute, and the expected variation. A question about one fixed fact is not statistical.

examples.q: Is “How many centimeters are in one meter?” statistical? Explain.
examples.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

examples.q: A survey asks “Is our school nice?” Improve it to collect numerical data with expected variation.
examples.a: Example: On a 1 to 5 scale, how do students in our class rate the school library? Ratings vary among students; the numerical scale must be defined.
examples.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Is “How many pages did each student read last night?” statistical? Explain.
problems.a: Yes; pages read vary across students.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Is “How many centimeters are in one meter?” statistical? Explain.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.a: Group: class; attribute: sleep duration; units: minutes.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Rewrite “How long is my pencil?” as a statistical question.
problems.a: Example: What are the lengths in centimeters of the pencils in our classroom?
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: A student asks only one person’s age once. Explain why “How old is this person today?” is not statistical.
problems.a: It seeks one fixed value, rather than anticipating variation in a data collection.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Write a statistical question about travel to school. Name the group, attribute, units, and why answers may vary.
problems.a: Example: How many minutes do students in our class take to reach school? Group: class; travel time in minutes varies with routes and travel methods.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: A survey asks “Is our school nice?” Improve it to collect numerical data with expected variation.
problems.a: Example: On a 1 to 5 scale, how do students in our class rate the school library? Ratings vary among students; the numerical scale must be defined.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Plan a class investigation of daily water use. Write a statistical question, identify a unit, and describe how to collect comparable data.
problems.a: Example: How many liters of water do students in our class drink in one day? Record each student’s total over the same 24-hour period in liters; amounts can differ.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

problems.q: Critique: “A question is statistical whenever it contains numbers.” Give a counterexample and a corrected rule.
problems.a: Counterexample: How many sides does a triangle have? It has a fixed answer. A statistical question anticipates variability in a collection of data.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

days.title: Designing a School Garden
days.target: I can use coordinates and polygon areas to plan a garden.
days.lecture: Read the requested quantity first and identify the relevant model. Plot vertices in order and connect them, including the last to the first. Equal x-values make a vertical side; equal y-values make a horizontal side. Count or subtract coordinates to get the side lengths. Explain why the units and the final value fit the situation.

examples.q: Sketch a triangle with base 4 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. Find its area.
examples.steps: A = bh/2 = 4 × 6 ÷ 2 = 12. Two such triangles make a parallelogram.

examples.q: A trapezoid has parallel bases 12 m and 22 m and perpendicular height 4 m. Sketch it and find its area.

problems.q: Plot and connect (0,0), (10,0), (10,9), (0,9). Find the side lengths and area.
problems.steps: Horizontal length 10 - (0) = 10; vertical length 9 - (0) = 9; area = 10 × 9.

problems.q: Sketch a triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 2 cm. Find its area.
problems.steps: A = bh/2 = 12 × 2 ÷ 2 = 12. Two such triangles make a parallelogram.

problems.q: An L-shaped garden is a 12 m by 9 m rectangle with an 8 m by 5 m corner rectangle removed. Sketch and find the garden area.
problems.steps: Outer area 108 minus cutout 40 = 68.

Plot and connect (-2,-3), (5,-3), (5,5), (-2,5). Find the side lengths and area.
problems.steps: Horizontal length 5 - (-2) = 7; vertical length 5 - (-3) = 8; area = 7 × 8.

problems.q: Sketch a triangle with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
problems.steps: A = bh/2 = 6 × 7 ÷ 2 = 21. Two such triangles make a parallelogram.

problems.q: A 10 m by 9 m rectangle has a right-triangle corner removed with perpendicular legs 6 m and 3 m. Sketch the remaining polygon and find its area.
problems.steps: Whole rectangle 90; remove triangle 9; difference 81.

problems.q: A trapezoid has parallel bases 10 m and 16 m and perpendicular height 2 m. Sketch it and find its area.
Plot and connect (-7,-6), (3,-6), (3,3), (-7,3). Find the side lengths and area. Find the perimeter too.
problems.a: Sides 10 and 9; area 90 square units; perimeter 38 units
problems.steps: Horizontal length 3 - (-7) = 10; vertical length 3 - (-6) = 9; area = 10 × 9.

problems.q: Sketch a triangle with base 14 cm and perpendicular height 7/2 cm. Find its area. Explain why the slanted side is not needed.
problems.steps: A = bh/2 = 14 × 7/2 ÷ 2 = 49/2. Two such triangles make a parallelogram.

days.title: Planning Storage and Packaging
days.target: I can connect volume and nets to compare storage designs.
days.lecture: Read the requested quantity first and identify the relevant model. A rectangular prism has volume V = lwh = Bh, where B is base area. Fractional edge lengths still multiply. Use cubic units; surface area and volume measure different attributes. Explain why the units and the final value fit the situation.

examples.q: Fill a prism 3/2 × 2 × 1 units with cubes of edge 1/2 unit. How many cubes fit? Use their volumes to verify lwh.
examples.a: 24 cubes; each 1/8 cubic unit; prism 3 cubic units
examples.steps: Counts along edges: 3, 4, 2. Product 24; 24 × 1/8 = 3, also lwh.

examples.q: Draw a net for a triangular prism. Its two congruent right-triangle bases have legs 3 cm and 4 cm and hypotenuse 5 cm; prism length is 8 cm. Label all faces and find surface area.
examples.steps: Triangle pair: 12 cm²; rectangles: (3+4+5) × 8 = 96; total 108.

problems.q: A rectangular prism has edges 7, 2, and 6 cm. Sketch it and find its volume.
Fill a prism 5/2 × 7/2 × 2 units with cubes of edge 1/2 unit. How many cubes fit? Use their volumes to verify lwh.
problems.a: 140 cubes; each 1/8 cubic unit; prism 35/2 cubic units
problems.steps: Counts along edges: 5, 7, 4. Product 140; 140 × 1/8 = 35/2, also lwh.

problems.q: Draw a net for a closed 8 × 3 × 5 cm rectangular prism. Label the six faces and calculate total area.
A 5 cm by 6 cm base and 5 cm height form a closed box. Draw its net and find the material area. Ignore tabs and overlap.
problems.steps: Closed surface area = 2(30+25+30) = 170.

problems.q: A square pyramid has base edge 10 cm. Each triangular face has perpendicular face height 12 cm. Draw a net and calculate total surface area.
problems.steps: Base = 100; each triangle = 10 × 12 ÷ 2 = 60; add four triangles to get 340.

problems.q: A rectangular prism has edges 4, 1 1/2, and 3 cm. Sketch it and find its volume.
Fill a prism 2/3 × 1 × 2 units with cubes of edge 1/3 unit. How many cubes fit? Use their volumes to verify lwh.
problems.a: 36 cubes; each 1/27 cubic unit; prism 4/3 cubic units
problems.steps: Counts along edges: 2, 3, 6. Product 36; 36 × 1/27 = 4/3, also lwh.

problems.q: Draw a net for a triangular prism. Its two congruent right-triangle bases have legs 3 cm and 4 cm and hypotenuse 5 cm; prism length is 2 cm. Label all faces and find surface area.
problems.steps: Triangle pair: 12 cm²; rectangles: (3+4+5) × 2 = 24; total 36.

problems.q: A 8 cm by 7 cm base and 6 cm height form an open-top box. Draw its net and find the material area. Ignore tabs and overlap.
problems.steps: Closed surface area = 2(56+48+42) = 292. Remove the top area 56: 236.

problems.q: A square pyramid has base edge 6 cm. Each triangular face has perpendicular face height 10 cm. Draw a net and calculate total surface area. Explain why the vertical pyramid height is not needed.
problems.steps: Base = 36; each triangle = 6 × 10 ÷ 2 = 30; add four triangles to get 156.

problems.steps: Box runs from 5 to 7, median line at 11/2, whiskers to 4 and 16.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 20. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
problems.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Median 19/2 min, IQR 2 min; right-skewed with a high value 20 min, so median/IQR resist that value.
problems.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.

problems.q: Critique: “A question is statistical whenever it contains numbers.” Give a counterexample and a corrected rule.
problems.a: Counterexample: How many sides does a triangle have? It has a fixed answer. A statistical question anticipates variability in a collection of data.
problems.steps: Look for a collection of data and anticipated variation; identify the population and variable.

days.title: Connecting Models and Explanations
days.target: I can select models and explain geometric and statistical results.
days.lecture: Read the requested quantity first and identify the relevant model. Two matching triangles form a parallelogram, so A = (base × perpendicular height)/2. A slanted side is not necessarily the height. Label area in square units. Explain why the units and the final value fit the situation.

examples.q: A rectangular prism has edges 2, 3, and 4 cm. Sketch it and find its volume.
Reading times in minutes are 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 15. Find the five-number summary and draw a labeled box plot. State the IQR.
examples.steps: Box runs from 4 to 6, median line at 9/2, whiskers to 3 and 15.

problems.q: Sketch a triangle with base 16 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Find its area.
problems.steps: A = bh/2 = 16 × 5 ÷ 2 = 40. Two such triangles make a parallelogram.

problems.q: A rectangular prism has edges 5, 2 1/2, and 2 cm. Sketch it and find its volume.
A 5 cm by 4 cm base and 5 cm height form a closed box. Draw its net and find the material area. Ignore tabs and overlap.
problems.steps: Closed surface area = 2(20+25+20) = 130.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 6, 9, 9, 12, 12, 15. Describe a typical value, range, shape, and any striking value.
problems.a: Center near 21/2 min; range 9 min; roughly symmetric; no isolated extreme
problems.steps: The values balance around the middle. Range = 15 - 6.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 6, 9, 9, 12, 12, 15. Report n, units, and mean.
Reading times in minutes are 8, 13, 13, 18, 18, 23. Find Q1, Q3, IQR, and range.
problems.a: Q1 13, Q3 18; IQR 5 min; range 15 min
problems.steps: Lower half [8, 13, 13] has median 13; upper half [18, 18, 23] has median 18. Subtract Q1 from Q3.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 18. Calculate the mean and MAD. Show all absolute deviations. Interpret MAD in a sentence.
problems.a: Mean 55/6 min; MAD 53/18 min; a typical distance from the mean is 53/18 min

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 14. Find the five-number summary and draw a labeled box plot. State the IQR.
problems.steps: Box runs from 3 to 5, median line at 7/2, whiskers to 2 and 14.

problems.q: Reading times (min): Group A [6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 18], Group B [8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 20]. Compare median and IQR. Which group reads longer typically? Which is more consistent?
problems.a: A median 15/2, B median 19/2 min; both IQR 2 min. B is typically 2 min higher; equal middle-half variability.
problems.steps: Adding 2 shifts all values and the median by 2, but does not change Q3 - Q1.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 14. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
problems.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Median 7/2 min, IQR 2 min; right-skewed with a high value 14 min, so median/IQR resist that value.
problems.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.

days.title: Final Review Quiz
days.target: I can apply the skills taught so far, show my reasoning, and check my answers.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10. Draw a labeled dot plot. Check the number of dots.
problems.steps: Each observation contributes one dot; stack repeated values at their number-line position.

problems.q: A trapezoid has parallel bases 10 m and 14 m and perpendicular height 4 m. Sketch it and find its area.
A rectangular prism has edges 1, 3, and 4 cm. Sketch it and find its volume.
Reading times in minutes are 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 16. Find the five-number summary and draw a labeled box plot. State the IQR.
problems.steps: Box runs from 5 to 7, median line at 11/2, whiskers to 4 and 16.

problems.q: Reading times in minutes are 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 17. Write a summary with count, attribute, units, center, variability, shape, and a justified choice of measures.
problems.a: 6 observations of reading time in minutes. Median 13/2 min, IQR 2 min; right-skewed with a high value 17 min, so median/IQR resist that value.
problems.steps: Calculate the center and spread before interpreting them in context. Other accurate, justified summaries are acceptable.

6.RP.A.1.description: Describe multiplicative ratio relationships using clear labels and ratio language.

6.RP.A.2.description: Interpret unit rates and state what the rate per one unit means.

6.RP.A.3a.description: Use tables, missing values, graphs, and comparisons of equivalent ratios.

6.RP.A.3c.description: Solve percent situations with the part, whole, or rate unknown.

6.NS.A.1.description: Interpret and compute fraction quotients with equations and visual models.

6.NS.B.2.description: Use the standard algorithm to divide multi-digit whole numbers fluently.

6.NS.B.3.description: Use standard algorithms for all four operations with decimals.

6.NS.B.4a.description: Find greatest common factors with whole numbers no greater than 100.

6.NS.B.4b.description: Find least common multiples with whole numbers no greater than 12.

6.NS.B.4c.description: Factor a sum using a common factor and the distributive property.

6.NS.C.5.description: Represent opposite real-world quantities with signs and explain zero.

6.NS.C.6a.description: Recognize opposites, double opposites, and zero as its own opposite.

6.NS.C.6b.description: Connect coordinate signs with quadrants and axis reflections.

6.NS.C.6c.description: Locate rational numbers on number lines and coordinate planes.

6.NS.C.7b.description: Explain order comparisons in real-world contexts.

6.NS.C.7c.description: Interpret absolute value as distance or magnitude.

6.NS.C.7d.description: Distinguish order comparisons from comparisons of magnitude.

6.NS.C.8.description: Graph in four quadrants and use coordinates to find aligned distances.

6.EE.A.1.description: Write and evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents.

6.EE.A.2a.description: Translate operations involving numbers and variables into expressions.

6.EE.A.2b.description: Name terms, sums, factors, products, quotients, and coefficients.

6.EE.A.2c.description: Evaluate expressions and formulas in the correct operation order.

6.EE.A.3.description: Use operation properties to generate equivalent expressions.

6.EE.A.4.description: Determine and justify whether expressions are equivalent.

6.EE.B.5.description: Use substitution to determine whether a value satisfies an equation or inequality.

6.EE.B.6.description: Define and use variables for unknown or varying numbers in context.

6.EE.B.7.description: Solve addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division one-step equations with nonnegative rational values.

6.EE.B.8.description: Write and graph strict and inclusive inequalities; recognize infinitely many solutions.

6.EE.C.9.description: Relate two changing quantities using equations, tables, and graphs.

6.G.A.1.description: Find polygon areas through composition and decomposition.

6.G.A.2.description: Connect fractional unit-cube packing with right rectangular prism volume.

6.G.A.3.description: Draw coordinate polygons and calculate horizontal and vertical side lengths.

6.G.A.4.description: Draw nets and use face areas to calculate surface area.

6.SP.A.1.description: Recognize questions that anticipate variability in collected data.

6.SP.A.2.description: Describe distributions by center, spread, and overall shape.

6.SP.A.3.description: Distinguish measures of center from measures of variability.

6.SP.B.4.description: Construct and interpret dot plots, histograms, and box plots.

6.SP.B.5b.description: Name the investigated attribute, measurement method, and units.

6.SP.B.5c.description: Summarize center and variability and explain patterns or unusual values in context.

6.SP.B.5d.description: Choose center and variability measures suited to the distribution and context.
